content: Abdominal tuberculosis (TB) refers to TB infection involving the gastrointestinal tract or other organs within the abdominal cavity. Current guidelines generally recommend a six-month treatment regimen, similar to that used for pulmonary TB. However, there is concern among some physicians that six months may not be sufficient to prevent relapse, particularly in cases of gastrointestinal TB, where drug absorption may be compromised. On the other hand, extending the treatment duration could lead to poor adherence, increased relapse rates, the development of drug resistance, and higher costs for both patients and healthcare systems. The objective of this study was to compare the efficacy of six-month versus longer treatment regimens for abdominal TB. The researchers conducted a systematic search of multiple electronic databases up to September 2, 2016, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, PubMed, Embase, LILACS, INDMED, and the South Asian Database of Controlled Clinical Trials. They also searched the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform and ClinicalTrials.gov for ongoing trials and reviewed reference lists of relevant articles. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared six-month regimens with longer regimens (e.g., nine months) for treating abdominal TB in adults and children. The regimens consisted of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, administered either daily or thrice weekly under directly observed therapy (DOT). The primary outcomes assessed were relapse rates (with a minimum follow-up of six months after treatment completion) and clinical cure rates at the end of treatment. Three RCTs involving 328 participants were included in the analysis. All trials were conducted in Asia and excluded individuals with HIV, co-morbidities, or prior antituberculous treatment within the last five years. The median follow-up duration after treatment completion ranged from 12 to 39 months. Relapse was rare, with two cases reported among 140 participants treated for six months and no cases among 129 participants treated for nine months. However, due to the small sample size, it remains unclear whether there is a significant difference in relapse risk between the two regimens (very low-quality evidence). At the end of therapy, there was likely no difference in the proportion of participants achieving clinical cure between the six-month and nine-month regimens (risk ratio [RR] 1.02, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.97 to 1.08; 294 participants, 3 trials; moderate-quality evidence). Regarding mortality, two deaths occurred in the six-month group (2/150, 1.3%) and four in the nine-month group (4/144, 2.8%). All deaths occurred within the first four months of treatment and were unrelated to treatment duration. Similarly, treatment default rates were low in both groups, with no significant difference observed (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.10 to 2.59; 294 participants, 3 trials; low-quality evidence). Adherence to treatment was reported in only one trial, where one participant in the nine-month group demonstrated poor adherence. It is uncertain whether six-month regimens are associated with fewer adverse events leading to treatment interruption (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.18 to 1.55; 318 participants, 3 trials; very low-quality evidence). In conclusion, the available evidence does not suggest that six-month treatment regimens are inadequate for treating intestinal and peritoneal TB. No additional benefits of nine-month regimens were observed in terms of relapse prevention or clinical cure rates. However, the small sample size and low quality of evidence limit confidence in these findings. Further research, including larger studies with long-term follow-up and the inclusion of HIV-positive individuals, is needed to draw more definitive conclusions about the safety and efficacy of six-month treatment regimens for abdominal TB.
